newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end higher, technology stocks rebound.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end higher, technology stocks rebound.

text.p: U.S. stocks ended higher on Wednesday, fueled by strong oil and technology sectors, but moderately restrained by concerns about higher interest rates.
A day after the Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates for the first time in two years, the Dow industrials closed at 6880.70, up 4.53 points.
Advancing issues narrowly beat declines on the New York Stock Exchange.
In contrast, the technology heavy Nasdaq composite index sizzled, soaring 21.01 to 1269.07.
"For the first time in quite a while, the big tech stocks pulled up the Nasdaq," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham.
Intel Corp, Cisco Systems Inc and Microsoft Corp gained sharply. Intel rose 7-3/8 to 140-5/8, jumped 4-1/2 to 52-3/8, while software giant Microsoft rose 3-15/16 to 94-1/4.
On the Big Board, IBM rose 4-1/2 to 140-5/8, while Motorola advanced 3-5/8 to 62 after announcing contracts with two Japanese wireless phone operators.

In the oil sector, Exxon Corp surged 3-1/2 to 109-3/8 after the company said on Tuesday that it plans to increase share buybacks. Other oil stocks rose, with Chevron Corp up 1/2 to 72-1/8 and Texaco Inc up 1-3/8 to 109-3/8.
For the most part, though, the technology rebound did not spread to the rest of the market.
"We had a reversal in the malaise in the technology sector, but it did not rub off on the rest of the market," said Kugel.
Kugel said the market would remain in its current range.

"Between Election Day in 1996 and February 15 this year, we had a tremendous surge on strong corporate earnings and a stronger than expected economy," said Kugel. "Now the market is in a digestion period.
But Harry Laubscher, market analyst at Tucker Anthony, said the market could see a brief rally.
"The star of the day was the Nasdaq," he said. "We're starting to (register) a short-term buy in that index, which suggests that we will probably see further gains in those technology stocks."

Laubscher said a strong technology sector could provide some leadership to the Dow. As a consequence, he said: "We could get a brief rally -- maybe for a week or two -- before we get some new selling pressures."

A day after the Fed tightened monetary policy, however, the markets were hardly free of interest-rate worries. The bond market weakened, if moderately. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield rose to 6.99 percent. And rate-sensitive financial stocks fell. Chase Manhattan Corp shed 1-7/8 to 99-7/8, BankAmerica Corp dipped 2-3/4 to 109-1/4 and Morgan Stanley Group Inc dropped 1-3/4 to 62-3/8.
Viacom Inc fell 3-3/8 to 32-1/2 and Young Broadcasting Inc dropped five to 22-1/4 after Merrill Lynch lowered its near-term ratings on the stocks.

A Lehman Brothers analyst raised his first quarter earnings estimates on several U.S. airlines, citing potentially strong industry revenues. United Airlines parent UAL Corp rose three to 68, American Airlines parent AMR Corp gained 1-5/8 to 85-7/8 and Delta Air Lines Inc advanced 2-3/4 to 85-5/8.
PHAMIS Inc fell 2-1/4 to 20 after saying it agreed to merge with IDX Systems Corp, a provider of healthcare information systems. IDX fell 3-3/4 to 28.
The S&P 500 index rose 1.43 to 790.50.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 21.02 points to 1269.08.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
